segments.narration: A single river mouth gets hit by lightning thousands of times on active nights. Over Venezuela’s Lake Maracaibo, lightning strikes for nine hours straight.
For centuries, Caribbean sailors used this unnatural glow as a lighthouse. Ancient legends blamed fire spirits, while early scientists were stumped.
segments.visual_query: caribbean sea historic sailing ship night

segments.narration: How does one sky re-arm the exact same storm every night? While nearby towns sleep under starlight, this lone valley explodes.
Researchers found the secret: moist winds smash into the surrounding Andes, forcing warm air upward and generating massive atmospheric charges.
Geography and mountain wind patterns created a permanent natural electrical generator. If global wind patterns shift, could this ancient lightning lighthouse finally flicker out?

accuracy_flags.claim: The Catatumbo River mouth in Venezuela experiences up to twenty thousand lightning strikes in a single night.
accuracy_flags.note: The phenomenon occurs 140 to 160 nights a year (not every night) for about nine hours per day (not ten). Additionally, Catatumbo translates to 'House of Thunder', contradicting the claim of silent lightning.

accuracy_flags.claim: Trade winds crashing into the Andes mountains combined with methane from local marshes cause the Catatumbo lightning.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference explicitly notes that the methane model is contradicted by the observed behavior of the lightning across wet and dry seasons.

accuracy_flags.claim: The Catatumbo lightning storm is driven by regional wind circulation and marshland methane release.
accuracy_flags.note: Attributing the phenomenon to swamp gas (methane) presents a contradicted hypothesis as fact.
